extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans of television/comedy, and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of the British sitcom Blackadder
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article summarising the British television sitcom Blackadder: its premise, series-by-series settings, production history, casting, specials, music, reception and legacy. The page provides descriptive and historical information rather than prescriptive how-to guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series format and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Each series comprises six half-hour episodes and is set in a different period of British history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists the four main series (The Black Adder, Blackadder II, Blackadder the Third, Blackadder Goes Forth) and their historical settings (e.g., fictional Richard IV/late 15th century; Elizabeth I; the Regency; World War I). Use of distinct historical periods is a structural device for the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production cost and shooting method (studio vs location)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the BBC's request for improvements (and a severe budget reduction), several changes were made. To reduce the cost of production, it was shot with virtually no outdoor scenes and several frequently used indoor sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts the first series' ambitious location shooting and large budgets with later series' studio-only approach and repeated indoor sets; producers cut costs by using studio recordings and a live audience to improve comedic consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live audience recording
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackadder II was the first to be recorded with a live audience during recording, instead of showing the episodes to an audience after taping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shift to live-audience recording was part of the retooling to improve comedy timing and audience response; it's presented as an intentional production decision to increase comedic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character dynamics for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Elton suggested a major change in character emphasis: Baldrick would become the stupid sidekick, while Edmund Blackadder evolved into a cunning sycophant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change in the protagonist/sidekick relationship is described as central to establishing the familiar Blackadder character and improving the show's comedic focus; it serves as guidance on character design for period sitcom comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anachronism and dramatic licence
rubrics_metrics.description: Many historical events portrayed in the series were anachronistic (for example, Constantinople had already fallen to the Ottoman Empire in 1453, predating the events in the episode by 32 years); this dramatic licence would continue in the three subsequent Blackadder series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents anachronism and alternative-history elements as deliberate comedic tools—writers take liberties with historical accuracy for satire and humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: blending comedy with darker/poignant themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The series' tone [particularly Blackadder Goes Forth] is somewhat darker than the previous three series; it details the privations of trench warfare as well as the incompetence and life-wasting strategies of the top brass. The final episode, 'Goodbyeee', is known for being extraordinarily poignant for a comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry highlights that a sitcom can incorporate darker subject matter and end on a poignant note—using wartime context to blend satire with genuine emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical theme continuity adapted by period
rubrics_metrics.description: Howard Goodall's theme tune has the same melody through all the series, but is played in roughly the style of the period in which it is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: trumpets/timpani for The Black Adder (medieval), recorder/string quartet/electric guitar for Blackadder II, oboe/cello/harpsichord for Blackadder the Third, military band for Blackadder Goes Forth. Keep thematic continuity while varying instrumentation to evoke each period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and recurring/variant roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Each series tended to feature the same set of regular actors in different period settings, although throughout the four series and specials, only Blackadder and Baldrick were constant characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes a casting pattern where actors reappear across series in different incarnations (e.g., Tim McInnerny, Stephen Fry, Hugh Laurie), providing continuity while allowing role variation—useful casting strategy for anthology-like period sitcoms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode length and series length conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each series comprises six half-hour episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consistent episode count and runtime is presented as the show's structural convention—useful as a model for similar period sitcom productions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary/shakespearean stylings for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The series also featured Shakespearean dialogue, often adapted for comic effect; the end credits featured the words 'Additional Dialogue by William Shakespeare'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting period-appropriate (or faux-period) diction and known literary styles can heighten humour through contrast and parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode naming as period-appropriate wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: The episode titles were puns on Jane Austen's novels Sense and Sensibility and Pride and Prejudice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using punning or intertextual episode titles tied to the era's literature is a recurrent playful device in the series' writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition vs. comedic consistency trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: The first series was odd, it was very extravagant. It cost a million pounds for the six programmes ... It looked great, but it wasn't as consistently funny as we would have liked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames a production lesson: high production values and ambition (location shooting, large cast, elaborate costumes) can produce great visuals but may not guarantee consistent humour; later adjustments prioritized comedic consistency over extravagance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specials and format flexibility tied to funding/partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in the Back & Forth millennium special was the shooting once again on location, because this was a production with a budget estimated at £3 million, and was a joint venture between Tiger Aspect, Sky Television, the New Millennium Experience Company and the BBC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specials may depart from series conventions (location shooting, higher budgets) when additional funding or partnerships enable it; format can therefore be flexible depending on resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural reception and longevity as evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackadder Goes Forth ranked at 16 in the 100 Greatest British Television Programmes (BFI); Edmund Blackadder was ranked third in Channel 4's 100 Greatest TV Characters; in a 2004 TV poll Blackadder (all four series combined) was voted the second-best British sitcom of all time; ranked as the ninth-best TV show by Empire magazine in 2009.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses polls, rankings and critical lists as measures of the show's impact and quality; cultural penetration (memorable quotes, stamps, revivals/specials) is also treated as evidence of success.
